Dwarf Fortress has been out for 20 years. For three quarters of those twenty years, I have been playing Dwarf Fortress. Not consistently, sometimes going years on without playing it, but I've been there. I have a lot of opinions from thousands of hours of gameplay, and I've bought the game four times now, thrice sending money directly to Bay 12 as a donation. I'm proudly on the wall of champions, and I don't regret that purchase.

Here's the TL;DR. Dwarf Fortress is a massive game with a glacial development speed, questionable design choices, and it is not for everyone at such a core level that you might not even understand if it is for you or not after hundreds of hours of gameplay. It's more of a personal belief than a real true or false statement. But it is for me, or maybe it was, and I just haven't realized I've moved on from it yet.

Alright, so here's the thing. Dwarf Fortress has changed massively in these last twenty years, and I can't deny it, but I also can't say that I agree with every single change made. I can't say that I agree with some older changes, and also some newer changes. Things like removing keyboard controls, or focusing on graphics over enhancing the gameplay as things continue to be worked on. I can't agree with how difficult modding has become with the changes to visuals. I don't even know if I agree with the new music, but I'll say that I am just being curmudgeonly on that regard, and resistant to change. 

Some of the artwork that's come out of the game is just downright atrocious, and I understand that it's just some artist's style, but there really should be some revisions done on a few of the animals and animal people. Some really got hit badly by the ugly stick. I understand that art is a major reason why development has slowed to an utter crawl even compared to before, but just throwing up the first pass and calling it done is a disservice to the game. Thankfully, mods exist, so it's a lesser issue. (EDIT: They may have done more passes on these recently. Take this with a grain of salt, but it's all opinion anyway.)

I don't know if I agree with the decision to go with Kitfox as a publisher. I have a distrust for them due to some of their past actions when handling certain games, as well as for their stance on "fantastical racism", which is a very overburdened term for light-hearted ribbing of elves and goblins. It's kind of rich when dealing with a game that has its characters genetically predisposed to disliking other civilizations straight out of the womb. I'm not sure if it's an attempt to beat down grognards like myself to open the community up for new blood, or if it's just overzealous moderation, but it's a bit much.

And no, this isn't about gay dwarves and livestock. People up in arms over that need to get real, at worst it's annoying to deal with a gay cow, but gay meat is still as edible as straight meat, just butcher the thing and get a new one on the next caravan.

Further to that, Kitfox has seemed to be going down the road of tie-in media and bombastic advertising. I feel like they're trying to make Tarn into a character, or a caricature of himself, rather than having him just be a down-to-earth guy like his postings on the forums would suggest. When I saw the phrase "Tarn Time" show up on my feed, I just about flipped my lid at the pure marketing vomitus. "It's called Future of the Fortress you apes! What are you doing?!" I screamed. And when I saw the magic the gathering tie-in set, I sincerely considered slamming my face through my desk.

But maybe I'm just old. The 20s have been a decade of new publishing houses making deals left and right, and the corporations of old are still trying to hold onto power. I wouldn't be surprised if I saw a netflix series on Dwarf Fortress, but I might be shocked if I saw Dwarf Fortress vs Skibidi Toilet toys at Wal-Mart. Please do not let this happen.

So, that's the more nebulous part of my rant done. Here's some actual information on the game.

The most important thing to remember is this. Dwarf Fortress is not difficult. It's complex, but not difficult. Rimworld is more difficult, whereas Dwarf Fortress is more random and layered. The worst enemy you will face in Dwarf Fortress is yourself, because you'll get bored or tired, and either kill your own fort or retire it. You need to be okay with that, the constant cycle of start-build-refine-repeat, and learn to enjoy the differences each fort will have, rather than the challenge of the game itself. As the wise men say, "Losing is Fun". You'll have your best moments in the end of your days, and the rest is just building up to that point.

As for development, it's what I would call very consistently glacial. Tarn said recently that there will be no more "Big Waits" between updates. That's sort of true, but I would also argue that there never really were if we count bugfixes and minor additions. You will have to wait on the order of years between major updates, but you have to know that Tarn (and Zach, at times) and all of their contractors are working and refining and working some more, and that every update is worth the wait. Dwarf Fortress, in all of my memory, has never released an update half-baked. They're always beyond quality.

Like I said, you will play this game in cycles if you love it. It'll call you back with its siren song just like it did to me. You'll hear a story, or read a combat log, or see a legends dump, or get a screenshot of a megastructure, and you'll get the itch. And that's all it takes. For me, the 20 year anniversary provided that itch. I had to let the game run for half an hour so I could write this review, or else I'd be stuck playing for hours, or days.

But in general, even if this game isn't for you, you'll get hours and hours out of it. Just in one big, long streak, and then you'll be done with it. It's like a diner, either you go for lunch once and have a good meal, or you get hooked and become a regular. Look at all the negative reviews, and you'll see most of them have 100+ hours. Some 1000+. Even the people who hate it can't help but keep going a bit more.

At the end of the day, that's why I've bought it four times. That's why I'm over a hundred dollars in the hole on this one game, and eighty of those dollars were spent when it was free. And I'd do it again in a heartbeat.

You might think I've complained so much that I have to give it a negative review. But I don't, and I won't. I complain so much because I've played this game to death and into unlife. It's a core component of my life, cracks and wrinkles and tears and all.

ORIGINAL REVIEW: I've been playing DF for years, and I don't mind throwing Bay12 some money for the first time after the thousands of hours I've spent playing this game, but this version is seriously lacking compared to the classic. I was under the impression that this would be a UI improvement with little change under the hood, but this version has been endlessly frustrating due to a bunch of nonsensical changes that aren't even in a changelog. 

Lots of tiny little things that a new player wouldn't notice have been removed. Doors can't be closed tightly to block animals, the simplified stair orders that don't allow the user to select stair type results in down stairs being dug when you want up/down. For example, I was try to punch through a aquifer and dwarves cancelled their orders, as they do, and then only dug down stairs when the dig orders are issued again because instead of being able to designate one stair construction the game now tries to decide for you what staircase you are trying to build based on your starting point. The same thing goes for probing caverns, pretty much the first milestone of the early game. If you penetrate the roof and want to cover your down stair while leaving the up stair to stop strange flying beasts from zooming up your staircase, you used to be able to just lay a floor. Now that destroys the up stair for some reason and traps your dwarf. Did anyone actually playtest this release?

Military/Hunting management has also been greatly simplified. Where did the ambush order go? Why can't I designate ammo use? You also no longer get a readout of the size of your designations. Have fun squinting and counting little yellow squares.

World gen parameters can no longer be exported through legends mode (your perfect random seed will never be seen again), and the new modding system (which I suspect was pushed by the publisher, Kitfox, who is weirdly gatekeeping their mod guide on Discord) has removed the capability to modify the game's raw files on the fly. A savvy player used to be able to switch things up mid game just by messing with some strings of text in the raws, a classic roguelike feature. Now you are ONLY allowed to apply mods at world generation, which is absolutely absurd considering how long it takes and how easy it used to be to say, remove an out-of-control aquifer drowning a perfect embark or mess with the color palette. Raws have been completely removed from save game folders and this is endlessly frustrating. Why? How hard is it to let me mess with dwarf hairstyles on the fly? What is the end game here? 

Many frustrating aspects that could have been worked on are still there too, but I won't fault them too much for that, it is DF. But with all the talk of improved dwarf labor priorities, why not make dwarves not prioritize constructions that block off access to other constructions designated in the same order? 

It's extremely disappointing that Bay12 has chosen to streamline the game at the cost of certain complexities. I have been playing since I was a little boy messing around in the elementary school computer lab looking for any game I could get for free. I have dived into every major release since 2010 with glee and spent weeks playing with my dwarves, but this release has left me nothing but frustrated and burnt out in a couple of days. 

This is just my little whackjob conspiracy theory, not really a part of the review, but it makes me wonder whether the Kitfox is really trying to steward the game to help it survive into a new era, or if they're deliberately sacrificing the beautiful micromanagement of DF for a ever-so-slightly dumber version for streamers and sales. Based on their pre-release projections, it seems like they did not have high hopes for the game, and a feature-cutting directive might have been pushed onto Bay12. Or maybe I just think too highly of Toady to think he's done wrong. Either way, I will be playing DF Classic until this is fixed or the negative changes are pushed onto that game.

It's not a game for everyone. Here's who should buy it and who shouldn't.

DO BUY DWARF FORTRESS IF... 

    (1)  you enjoy babysitting psychotic, alcoholic toddlers who love fighting each other and swigging plump helmet beer
    (2) you enjoy managing individuals have autistic focus on craftsmanship, digging holes, and reclaiming missing socks
    (3) you find humor in combat systems where dwarves who lose or break their weapons start headbutting and biting Forgotten Beasts
    (4) you are fascinated by geology, randomized world-building, and surprising emergent behavior
    (5) you are perpetually compulsive about what lies below in the next layer of dirt.
    (6) you are okay with the understanding that you can't control all your dwarves. They have minds of their own, and only do what you want them to do 70% of the time.
    (7) You are detail-oriented and enjoy pausing the game and (for fun!) flipping through stats, historical notes, and background information and other details for hours at a time.

DO NOT BUY IT IF....
    (1) You like clean, efficient interfaces to control game features. The game is much faster if you memorize keyboard shortcuts and learn where the dozens of submenus. It's a pretty opaque control system at first.
    (2) You like clear plotlines and goals. This is really more of a simulation than a game in the traditional sense, more akin to SimCity in that regard or the Sims.
   (3) You are the sort of Jenga player who gets frustrated when the Jenga pile gets more and more unstable. This game is a study in systems going out of control and crashing catastrophically, undoing what you spent hours laboriously building. You are never quite sure when a hole in your defenses will allow a Forgotten Beast to start a murderfest inside your fort, or when the emotionally unstable dude with the ax is going to lose it and start whacking dwarf children of his neighbors.
    (4) You like supermodern graphics and special effects. This game was originally run with ASCII code symbols and later on tile sets and only now has started getting what looks like 16 bit graphics. It is intentionally old-school and meant to exercise your imagination.
    (5) You like your games polished and finished. This one has been in construction for literally decades, and there are tons of "placeholder" features that are visible, but not yet fleshed out.

So far, I'm enjoying Dwarf Fortress, but I don't think it's everyone's mug of ale. If, however, you have the right compulsive personality, the right sense of humor, a good deal of patience, and a delight in detail, you might enjoy it.

This is a very addictive colony sim with an unrivaled amount of depth. Once you get a good grasp on how to keep your colony thriving and learn about most of the game's many sub-mechanics, you will begin to understand why people talk about this game with so much praise despite its flaws.

Concerning the flaws. I find it problematic that a big part of the community sweeps them under the rug. I won't do such a thing so let's address the main problems before we go to the good stuff:

- This game lacks a ridiculous amount of information on how to manage your colony. The tutorial barely covers a quarter of the core content of this game. I hate, hate, hate games that force players to rely on wikis. The wiki needs to be in the game, period. The game needs pop up info bubbles that are triggered when certain things happen for the first time. The game needs a codex. Many windows such as Dwarf profile require additional info for us to understand what's even going on.

- The user interface is very difficult to understand. There are many icons that do not explain visually what they exactly do. It is also quite ugly even for a 2D game.

- The game relies heavily on the modding community to make obvious quality of life content which is by definition wrong in my opinion. This includes the UI, visual polishing of the game, diversified icons and more.

- The game needs some animations and additional sounds to make it more lively and real. Animations shouldn't be too hard to do. Just 3 sprites for a dwarf drinking some ale could do the trick. You always hear the same sounds on loop on different floors depending on what you built. It's very annoying in the long run.

- The sprites move from one tile to the other. That is a problem, not just an aesthetic but also a practical one. Don't get me wrong - you will get over it after a short time though. It's all good up until you have a dwarf army and want to see the progression of the battle, or when you want to figure out the traffic movement of your dwarves when they are traveling from one place to the other to figure out if you could do something better to make them work faster. You can kinda guess their movement but it's just not fun. It is also very bothersome when many dwarves are on the same tile - for example during combat - and you're trying to figure out who's who.

- The game has so many features that some fall flat when you explore them and their impact on the game is minimal and more anecdotic than anything else. This is similar to Rimworld or Crusader Kings for example. Sometimes I wish those games would have more engaging stories that would be scripted. I think there could be room for both types.

- There are optimization issues with this game when you have many floors with many dwarves. The game will lag on your computer even if you can run current highly demanding games if you widen your fortress' map upon creating it. That is not normal and needs to be addressed.

There is also one thing that I believe falls between the positive and negative depending on how you view these types of games: The heavy randomization of things leave very little room for actual event structure, so it's just random things happening once in a while. Do not believe the Youtubers who come up with elaborate stories of their colony, they just make things up. That's not wrong per se but it can mislead some people into thinking there's an actual story here. A series of random events does not make a story unless you want it to.

Now for the good!

When I write a review for a game, it is usually because I have a lot to say about it. This review will include my major criticisms of the game, and I do so with love. I am not a long time fan and have never played the ASCII versions of the game. That being said, I LOVE this game. I practically can't shut up about it at home and with my friends. I want this game to succeed as much as it can. Dwarf Fortress is going to hit some people just right and become a staple in their gaming pastime for years at a time. I have been absolutely engrossed, entranced, dismayed and made to laugh so much from playing this game in the last 2 weeks. These beautiful moments happen in seemingly organic ways, making them feel special and original on your playthroughs, and often surprising you. The basic gameplay is not any more difficult than your typical sim management game. The devil is in the details.

There are tons of intricacies to the game that are not spelled out in the very succinct and few tutorials provided. The tutorials give you the gist of what any particular menu is for. However, if you are not used to having certain things not work intuitively and similarly to other games in the sim genre, or are not used to logic gate style controls for specific tasks, you are going to have a hard time fine-tuning how you produce certain outcomes.

It personally took me quite a bit of trial-and-error to understand how various objects in the game are categorized, and thus how stockpiles actually worked. Stockpiles are essential to playing, and the way it toggles and categorizes items is not entirely intuitive. When you get the hang of something like this, it can be a huge relief. Another thing is how there is this huge wiki that is a great resource online curated by fans for all sorts of things in the game, including many things I think should be included in the game. For instance: sometimes you are given demands by the Dwarves to construct certain types of areas related to their group, like a guild, temple complex, royal throne room, etc. There is no reference in the game that actually tells you what a temple complex or royal throne room is. There are many hints in the game that you may be able to infer what to do and reason backwards, which requires a lot of patience. A major example of this is how when you want to produce any good, but you don't already know what the recipe is, you have to queue it. You wait for the dwarf to go try to make the thing and then complain and cancel the order and tell you, "Needs x amount of thing". Now you know you need that thing, so you have to find what makes that thing, figure out how to source that thing's base ingredient, and spend time reorganizing your work force to sourcing that thing, building the workshop that processes that thing, and then getting it to the first dwarf. That is a lot of backwards reasoning , with writing on your notepad what to get, when it would be possible to include some way of seeing a recipe in the game on some reference sheet. Not my biggest complaint.

When it comes to the UI, DF comes down to menu management. Everything you do is text menus and scrolling across the map. I like a good menu. I like making "number go up" and looking at inventories. My issue with it is the ability to use the information on the menus and enter commands between menus is not fluid.

The windows for various menus can't be interacted with simultaneously, and can't be focused between with your mouse or with your keyboard in an easy way. You have to exit out of every menu before you can interact with another. On top of that, when there are circumstances where you can have two different windows/menus on the screen, the game doesn't always know which window you are trying to manipulate. This means that having your mouse hovered over one menu doesn't focus your UI, or often even by order of last menu you opened being the focused window. 

What this looks like: you will have two menu windows open taking up the majority of your screen but overlapping so you see one on top and the other partially, and your mouse wheel will more often than not scroll the map's Z-levels underneath the windows instead of the menus you have up. Since you can't tab between windows like you can a window manager (maybe there are just hotkeys but I am not sure) or have your cursor focus on a window, and instead have to close the window on top to interact with another, and there is information that is exclusive to different menus, you spend a lot of time opening and closing windows to check and correspond information and commands. You also can't resize them or manually move them as far as I can tell. They are in fixed positions.

There are toggles in these menus that will sort lists in different ways. Well, every time you exit out of a menu, the game resets each menu's sorting back to default way. This means if you want to reference information in lists a certain way, you have to click that toggle to your liking to sort it every time.

There might be something said for the game originally being made to use the keyboard predominantly and how you would manipulate the cursor, the visuals being originally pure ASCII, and it being so text-and-grid heavy. I can respect that. BUT, if you are going to launch it as a 1.0 on Steam and convert it with all the features for mouse usage with pixel graphic for mainstream users, this feels like an oversight. I'm not saying it is easy to develop a game, but it is a contemporary standard. The point of the features is to make management easier. I will admit that I am not going to remember every detail of information from these menus for reference to other menus for hundreds of little sprite people, nor am I likely to learn how to navigate DF's UI with the same attention & effort I would to learn how to use Vim without organically doing so over hundreds of hours with all the keybindings.

Since I’ve reached the 2,000-hour mark, I thought I should write a review.

This is going to leave a few people scratching their heads: “He has 2,000 hours but doesn’t recommend the game?”

There are six main problems I have with the game, which I would struggle to explain to someone new as to why they are still present after over 20 years of development as a passion project funded by fans, and 4 years on Steam as a company. It’s very much one of those games that a few people will love despite its problems, but most will hate because of them.

1. UI

The first, and most talked about, is the UI. There’s not much more I can say that hasn’t already been said, but in a strategy game specifically a city builder the UI is extremely important. Sadly, the UI is dated at best and poorly designed at worst.

I’m going to limit myself here since this has been discussed to death, but the most commonly voiced problems are: clunkiness (automation), too much information (character info), too little information (item info), and scaling issues (some menus being too big while others are too small).

From my understanding and feeling (hope), the current UI seems like a transitional system moving from the old free keyboard based version to a new, modern one.

2. Complexity and the strange lack of it

This is going to confuse a few people, since most reviews praise how complex and brilliant the game is and in many ways, it is.

For example: rock formations with layered geology and metal spawns, each organ of every creature being simulated, items having stats based on craftsmanship and metal/alloy even characters having likes, dislikes, relationships, and goals. That’s only a few examples.

The problem is that almost none of this is actually used. And when it is, it’s barely touched.

If you have a masterwork steel sword, all the stats temperature, durability, density, sharpness, crafter, etc. don’t really translate to much beyond “does a bit more damage and is worth more.” I’ve never seen a masterwork or normal steel sword go dull, rust, or break. In fact, I’ve only seen ever seen copper rust.

This applies to almost all items in the game: massive amounts of stats clogging up the system that mean almost nothing. The only thing I’ve ever seen lose durability is generic clothing, and craftsmanship or material doesn’t seem to matter there either. A leather shirt lasts just as long as a cloth shirt, whether it’s masterwork or normal. So what’s the point other than in your head lore?

3. The game feels half-baked in the late game

You become the breadbasket of your empire, or a weapon/armour factory producing legions worth of equipment, or maybe a grand library holding the world’s knowledge but what does that actually mean? What does it translate to in-game?

Do famine-stricken settlements request food? Nope. The entire import/export request system is RNG.

Surely, if you’re producing massive amounts of equipment, the king/queen would demand supplies for the empire’s army campains? Or adventurers would come to buy gear and slay mighty foes? Nope , no and before you ask no, it doesn’t matter if you have the entire world’s knowledge either.

The entire game is mostly what happens in your head, on the same level as a kid playing with plastic soldiers maybe slightly above that, since some things happen outside your fortress but it’s rarely anything interesting. Usually it’s just “X place got attacked.”

As a side note (trying to keep this small): not much happens inside your fortress either. Yes, there are murders, thefts, and raids but murders are usually just someone getting drunk and starting a fight then thefts are typically relics being stolen seemingly at random while raids aren’t much different from RimWorld.

Even with the siege update bringing things closer to RimWorld’s raid system, it still lacks the scale that DF should have. Yes, I know you can adjust the number of raiders, but it still boils down to four guys carrying a log.

4. The economy (or lack of one)

Fourth and this is my biggest disappointment is the economy or total lack of it. All the pieces are there, but it feels like a temporary system that became permanent.

Coins are the best example. We all know what coins are and what they’re used for. They exist in the game but they mean nothing. Ironically, most people who even bother to mint them do so purely for RP.

If you sell something worth 500 and buy something worth 400, you’d expect to get 100 coins back, right? Nope that extra value just disappears.

Surely coins are used to pay dwarves for their labour, and they buy goods? Nope. They just take what they need from storage.

Then maybe they use coins to buy missing goods from traders? Nope.

Do dwarves barter with each other? Nope.

There is zero internal economy. All trade goes through you.

You can have a fortress wealth in the trillions and it means nothing. Your dwarves aren’t wearing fancy exotic clothing bought from caravans. They just randomly grab clothes from storage even their likes and dislikes don’t affect what they wear at all.

5. Bugs

Fifth, and this will be short: bugs.

The game still has bugs that are over 10 years old. For a game being sold to still have the same bugs as the free version with bugs that have been around for years is unacceptable.

6. Lack of meaningful development

Sixth, the general lack of development.

Before anyone says “watch the YouTube videos, read the forums, sail the seven seas to see what’s being worked on” it’s not my job to hunt down developer updates I barely look at the steam patches even then it's normally like 6 things fixed.

Even with the siege update, which is marketed as the biggest update, all it really does is bring one system up to the level another game (RimWorld) has had at its release a game released 13 years ago.

Huge parts of the core game still shockingly dated and pointless. Between the release on steam and the current version, there’s almost no meaningful difference.

Final side note

Remove Adventure Mode from the marketing. The system is a proof of concept at best. It’s like Call of Duty marketing itself as a social media platform because you can talk via text and voice chat.

Including it in marketing feels like a deliberate attempt to make it seem like there’s more development than there actually is.

This game was the direct inspiration for Minecraft, Rimworld, Factorio, among many other gaming giants, and while all these games bring something special, none quite capture what Dwarf Fortress can bring.

Dwarf Fortress is a story generation game wearing the coat of a colony sim. Your creativity reigns supreme, and Dwarf Fortress does everything in its power to bring you dynamic storylines, chaos, and hilarious or terrifying situations. This is where many games, like Minecraft, falter because their core philosophy is to only ever react to the player. This creates static worlds, but Dwarf Fortress's worlds feel alive, dynamic, and chaotic in ways I have never seen before or since in a game.

Fair warning: this game is menu-heavy. If you like real-time immediate gameplay like Minecraft, then this may not be for you, but the game is truly interactive. It is not an idle or tycoon-kind of game.

Don't be worried about people calling this the "most difficult game to play ever." While it definitely has its rough edges (still in Alpha), it's nothing a quick 30-minute YouTube video can't fix. I recommend watching "THE ULTIMATE GUIDE TO DWARF FORTRESS" by VonGalactic and having the wiki open if you need it, and you'll be golden. Also, the whole ASCII graphics thing is not in this version; you have actual graphics and music here. Although, you can enable ASCII graphics if you want to vibe it out.

Speaking of this game still being in Alpha, that's actually a feature in my opinion! The game is alive and constantly getting new and huge updates. If you were there in the early Minecraft days, this game still feels like that. There is a real sense of constant excitement in the community about the development of this game, and the updates feel substantial. This has been ongoing for almost 20 years with no signs of stopping!

This game comes with three modes of play: Fortress Mode (the crux of the game), Legends Mode (an exhaustive log of every event, location, character, storyline, etc. of your generated worlds), and Adventure Mode. I won't explain Fortress Mode since the video I recommended above should do more than a good job of it.

Legends Mode, while not interactive, has tremendous value. If you play D&D, you can generate an entire world and use Legends Mode for your campaigns, or you can find inspiration in the logs for your next fantasy novel! It's also great for understanding what's actually happening in your world, where your dwarves come from, and who the major powers in your world are. It's easy to get lost in Legends Mode, and it's a welcomed, light addition to the game.

Adventure Mode is where my feelings for the game become complicated. In this mode, instead of managing a colony, you directly control a single character who has access to your entire world, including your existing fortresses. The premise is absolutely fantastic, play a role in your world, but in practice, the mode lacks major interactive features such as complex relationships, being a productive member of an existing fortress, fulfilling internal goals, or any sort of building mechanic. Improvements to the mode are planned but not in the foreseeable future. If the core premise sounds exciting to you, I recommend trying out another one of Kitfox's games, Caves of Qud.

Overall, Dwarf Fortress can easily become one of your most cherished gaming experiences. Call on Urist to grab his pickaxe, and Strike the Earth!

[b]HOT TAKES INCOMING:[/b]

1. [u]This game is should be listed as early access.[/u] It doesn't have a 1.0 release, is only ~0.5, and it shows. Hear me out:

2. [u]This game has many partially implemented features.[/u] Egg size exists but doesn't affect meal quantity. A chicken egg will feed as many dwarves are a giant dragon egg. Value in general needs (another) huge rework, currently if you engrave a metal floor or wall the room value is many times higher than anything else you can do. There are many balance issues like this.

3. [u]Weirdly opaque systems create an impression of difficulty for newcomers.[/u] It is common to run out of seeds. To solve this issue, you can research the wiki to see what production methods result in saving seeds or not. There is no clear in-game way to discover this. Another weird one is that cows need to be pastured with grass, but pigs can be kept in a single cell underground with zero need for ANY food. So if you want milk, the choice is obvious: Dig one underground cell for pig, milk pig. In the farming system the game gives an option of leaving the field fallow, which makes you think "WOW, crop rotation! They're simulating soil nitrogen content? Neat!" (Spoiler: Leaving the field fallow does nothing at all).

4. [u]This game has a ton of bugs.[/u] Go on the wiki and every second page you read will say "warning: this feature has significant bugs." Because of the issues above, it is difficult to tell if something is a bug or just poorly/partially implemented. Should wood flooring and walls be able to hold a reservoir of magma? Seems like a bug to me, but all constructions are indestructible so it might just be unfinished. Should large creatures be able to jump through fortifications, which are described as small slits carved in the wall you can shoot arrows through? Probably not, but they sure do! There are DECADE old bugs they haven't gotten around to fixing. For example, ahem,  Bug#2780 [i](from 2010)[/i]: "Weapons, especially whips, cut through steel armor like butter" is still active. It is both listed as a bug and an intended consequence of the weapon mechanics.

Yet you'll hear people online praising the material physics algorithms they're using. A silver whip effortlessly slices through steel plate; however, a silver edged weapon will barely scratch leather. Well, it is true that pure silver is very soft and can't hold an edge! But when you alloy it into harder sterling silver, it has the exact SAME properties as pure silver. Why even introduce alloying? [b]Is this a bug, incomplete, or unimplemented/intended? In dwarf fortress, it's usually some combination of all three.[/b]

5. Related final point: [u]the simulation is bad[/u]. Yes, everyone knows the drunken cat example. But did you know you can hold a reservoir of lava with a wooden floor and walls? Does that sound like a good simulation of temperature to you? But then a wooden drawbridge will deconstruct if it comes into contact with lava, as you'd expect. And almost anything can be trapped in cages, making them the optimal trap for almost all situations... Yes, that same cage suitable for a mouse can trap a giant ass dragon, it's all VERY silly.

Here's the story of my first fortress:

It was forged in the depths of the earth, carved into the rock by skilled and calloused hands. The dwarves dug tirelessly, creating tunnels, rooms, and grand halls. Water was diverted from an underground river, channeled into wells and cisterns, while forges and furnaces fueled the ambitions of the emerging kingdom. The heart of the fortress became a masterpiece: majestic columns supported carved ceilings, polished stone floors displayed concentric patterns, and temples dedicated to wealth, money, death, and lust took shape.
Aurora was only nineteen when she began mining. From a simple apprentice, she became a skilled miner, carving long tunnels into the depths. Her dedication was absolute, yet her heart longed for a place of retreat. Donor, the god of death, was her deity, and when the temple was completed, she became its acolyte, delighting the faithful with the sound of her lute. Her music echoed through the stone walls, bringing solace to those who paused to pray in the silent temple.
The goblin threat was constant. To defend against it, a long access corridor was built, narrow and flanked by sheer drops dozens of meters deep. At the bottom, a stagnant pool of water awaited any who fell. The passage was filled with pressure traps that triggered lethal falling boulders, while at the end of the corridor, behind a strategic corner, an armed militia awaited any survivors.
The attack came without warning. Two of the best warriors were outside, gathering wood. They saw the goblins and tried to fight, but they were outnumbered. As they were struck down by arrows, the enemy advanced. The corridor’s traps activated, killing only five invaders. The rest dodged the boulders and reached the entrance, cutting down the defending dwarves. Blood soaked the polished stones. One goblin stormed into the infirmary, where wounded dwarves, women, and children rested after the collapse of the grand entrance hall. The massacre was total. No one had time to scream. The base was compromised.
Aurora was in the underground worksites when she heard the first cries of alarm. Fleeing dwarves reached her, terror in their eyes was enough to make her understand. Torn between staying safe and fighting, it was hunger that drove her toward the food storage. She crossed the immense entrance hall, ascended the wide spiral staircase that wound upward for a hundred meters, avoiding the central corridors where the slaughter was still unfolding. The food storage was silent. Barrels and crates remained intact, but a pool of dried blood lay near the door. She ate quickly, then left, determined to help her companions. What she saw stopped her in her tracks: a pile of corpses, mutilated bodies of the elderly and children. An old miner ran aimlessly, an iron pickaxe clutched in his hands, yet without a single drop of blood on its metal. Fear had paralyzed him before he could use it. Tulon, one of the few remaining militia dwarves, stood next to a dying goblin, his axe buried in the enemy’s chest. "This is the last one," he said. But the price had been too high. The fortress was lost. Aurora and Tulon fled toward the underground worksites, determined to seal themselves inside and start anew. Behind them, surviving dwarves ran in desperation. But as they reached the atrium of the new subterranean citadel, they saw the terror etched on the faces of the fugitives. No one dared to go any further.
At the far end of the hall, a pool of black water was silently expanding. The well had failed the moment it was completed, just as the attack began. The underground river, diverted to supply the citadel, was flooding the lower levels. The new kingdom, the refuge, the dream of a fresh start, was about to be submerged.
No one knows what became of Aurora and Tulon. Some say they tried to dig an escape route, others that they walled themselves in the depths, becoming the guardians of a sunken kingdom. Their story is lost among the legends of a world now forgotten.

Dwarf Fortress is less a game you play than a complicated machine you gradually learn to interfere with.

At first, the difficulty mostly comes from the interface and from not knowing which of the games many systems you have accidentally neglected. You will spend twenty minutes figuring out how to perform an apparently simple task, confidently unpause the game, and discover that half your fortress is dying because you misunderstood something three hours earlier.

At some point something clicks though.

You stop seeing a collection of awkward menus and begin seeing a functioning little society. Your dwarves have jobs, preferences, relationships, grudges, pets, strange artistic tastes and an impressive ability to turn minor inconveniences into mass casualty events. You begin making plans. You build workshops, defenses, hospitals and elaborate infrastructure. You start feeling competent.

This is usually when the game kills fifty dwarves because sometimes that is just what happens. Should have found a way to kill the child that got bitten by a werelizard.

Once you have figured out the crucial systems, the game can become an exercise in optimization, but optimization for whatever you personally decide matters. You can optimize for efficiency, cruelty, wealth, military strength, architectural beauty, population growth, self-sufficiency or the production of an absurd number of finely crafted mugs. The game does not tell you what success should look like. It gives you a collection of interacting systems and lets you decide which numbers, outcomes or increasingly unnecessary megaprojects you care about. You make a plan and try to coerce your dwarfs into executing it.

My fortress has flooded because I misjudged an ice plug (3 times, how did I not realize that water freezes...), lost citizens to deadly dust from a forgotten beast (or maybe ichor? It sticks to your dwarfes...), produced several new werecreatures because I failed to contain the first infection quickly enough, and had an important artifact stolen by a visitor. At one point a bird stole my last cheese. The cheese wasnt important but it somehow felt personal.

These events do not feel like scripted quests. Dwarf Fortress is often described as a story generator, although at times it is closer to Mad Libs for D&D (thank you to whoever wrote that). The game supplies an enormous pile of characters, incidents and oddly specific details, while your brain does much of the work of turning them into a coherent tale.

When its systems collide just right, the resulting stories feel more personal and memorable than almost anything deliberately written for a game. Failure is rarely just a failed save. It becomes the history of a place that briefly worked before everything went catastrophically wrong.

The Steam version makes Dwarf Fortress much more approachable but “more approachable” is doing a lot of work here. The game still expects patience, curiosity and a willingness to look things up. Some information is buried, some controls are just not explained ingame, and some tasks remain far harder to perform than they have any right to be. There are moments when it feels less like commanding a fortress and more like operating ancient software whose original developer disappeared fifteen years ago. I'm still not sure where to collect clay or what certain icons actually mean.

And yet, once the machinery starts making sense, very few games offer anything comparable. The simulation is absurdly detailed, the procedural history gives the world genuine texture and the freedom to build, experiment, optimize and catastrophically miscalculate is enormous.

Dwarf Fortress is not welcoming. It does not respect your time in any conventional sense. It will confuse you, frustrate you and occasionally make you close the game after realizing that several hours of careful planning have ended in disaster.

Then, a little later, you might start wondering how the surviving dwarves are doing.

Highly recommended, provided you find the sentence “I wonder what terrible thing will happen if I try this” appealing.

We are successfully living a few seasons and becoming fat and happy and prosperous. Well everybody is happy except Cog Idenasrer a small child who took over my craft shop like it was his personal kingdom. I didn't think much of it because I do not even know how to use a craft shop yet.... but the behavior seemed somewhat odd? Check his stats... child is possessed by a demon. Ok? noob here I dunno wtf that even means. Focus on other stuff. Winter is coming. Stocked to the roof; mining commences. Winter is dragging on and we strike gold. Awesome. Everybody is pitching in to bring in this lustrous metal. The mood is one of drunken gaiety. The vein is large and the dwarves are working in a beautiful harmony with the mountain. Suddenly work is interrupted. The possessed child snaps. Goes insane and starts berserking. There is a huge commotion as he violently storms from room to room. There is an epic fight. It takes four adults and the bowyer's guinecock to subdue him in the main hall. He has been struck down. At the end of the fight he lays a mangled corpse in a pool of blood; his and everybody elses.

I will never forget my first dwarf dying on me. His name was Cog. Life goes on in an orderly fashion at Idengeb... for now...

This game is insane and did not disappoint.
Also it feels good to support the guys who made this amazing piece of art. Thanks for making it available for free for so many years and taking the time to make it accessible.
There is nothing else like it. This game is beautiful and it belongs in a museum.
